why: How a framework-reserved interaction verb ANSWERS, and which lane its answer travels on. `interactionSelect`/`interactionHover`/`clearSelection`/`selectAll`/`setSelectionMode`/`setGranularity` are ADMITTED by the dispatch turn with an empty `InvocationResult` plus an `Effect::SpawnJob`; the real result — `output.interactionView` and the app-declared refresh scope from `dispatch_interaction_action` — is published by the job's completion turn as `AppFrame::Invocation { in_reply_to: 0, .. }` (`plugin_complete_reserved_spawned_job`, `💻️os/🔨️modules/🔌️plugin/🦀️.rs`). Sequences start at 1, so `in_reply_to: 0` names NO caller: `AppChannelClient` cannot correlate that frame to any waiter and routes it to its `onOperationProgress` lane. A host that leaves it on the frame lane therefore never sees it — the wgpu browser target subscribes to that lane nowhere, so every pick answered the ADMISSION's empty scope, refreshed nothing, and the guest never republished `World3dScene.selectionJson`: a click selected on 7 of 8 generation3d examples in neither role (ticket 26/09/09/PROCEDURAL-3D-END-TO-END, `📓️wgpu-selection-roundtrip-2026-09-15.md`). React never saw it because its `deliverJobCompletionTurn` parks the same effects in the LEFTOVER lane, where `leftoverShellInvocationFrames` folds them. One lane rule, both hosts.

admission.why: What the dispatch turn resolves with: a reserved verb answers nothing itself, so its scope is the one that refreshes nothing.

settled.why: What the reserved job's completion turn publishes — the whole answer of the verb, on a frame that answers no command sequence.
